project.title: Lack of intestinal Mucin-1 impairs intestinal epithelial barrier and promotes metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in mice
project.projectDescription: Accumulating evidence suggests that a compromised intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) contributes to the progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD); however, the exact mechanisms remain unclear. Here we reveal that intestinal mucin 1 (MUC1) levels and glycosylation are decreased in both humans and mice with MASLD. Enterocyte-specific Muc1 knockout aggravates high-fat diet (HFD)-induced IEB impairment and MASLD progression in mice. Mechanistically, HFD feeding reduces the glycosylation of intestinal epithelial MUC1, triggering its clathrin-mediated endocytosis and NEDD4-mediated lysosomal degradation, which subsequently induces β-Catenin degradation and ultimately impaires the IEB. Notably, enterocyte-specific overexpression of cytoplasmic-tail-deleted MUC1 protects against IEB impairment and mitigates MASLD progression. These findings indicate that reduced intestinal epithelial MUC1 levels facilitate the progression of MASLD. Preserving the glycosylation and levels of intestinal MUC1 to maintain IEB integrity is a potential therapeutic strategy to explore for MASLD.
project.sampleProcessingProtocol: HT-29 cell lysates were immunoprecipitated with MUC1 antibody-conjugated Protein A+G agarose beads, washed three times with 1× TBS to remove non-specific binding. Bound complexes were eluted with 0.1% formic acid in 50% acetonitrile, neutralized with 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). Proteins were reduced with 10 mM DTT at 56°C for 45 min, alkylated with 55 mM iodoacetamide in dark at room temperature for 30 min, then quenched with excess DTT. Samples were diluted 1:5 with 25 mM ammonium bicarbonate, digested with trypsin (1:50 ratio) overnight at 37°C, and digestion terminated with 5% formic acid. Peptides were desalted using C18 spin columns, vacuum-dried, resuspended in 0.1% formic acid, and centrifuged at 14,000×g for 10 min. Supernatant was analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, with peptides separated on a C18 column using a 5-35% acetonitrile (0.1% formic acid) gradient over 90 min for MS/MS.
project.dataProcessingProtocol: Peptide samples were ionized by nanoelectrospray ionization and analyzed by tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode was used, with an initial MS resolution of 70,000 for intact peptides. Precursor peptides were selected for MS/MS using high-energy collision dissociation (HCD) at a normalized collision energy of 27, and fragment ions were detected at 17,500 resolution. The DDA procedure alternated between one MS scan and 15 MS/MS scans, targeting the most abundant precursors above 20,000 counts with 15-second dynamic exclusion. MS scans covered a mass range of 350-2000 Da.    Raw data were processed using Proteome Discoverer (ver. 1.3.0.339) to generate .mgf files, which were searched with Mascot (ver. 2.3.0) for peptide/protein identification. Searches were restricted to tryptic peptides, with carbamidomethylation (C) as a fixed modification and oxidation (M) plus Gln->pyro-Glu (N-term Q) as variable modifications. One missed cleavage was allowed, with precursor and fragment mass tolerances set to 10 ppm and 0.1 Da, respectively. Identified peptides were grouped into proteins, and results were retained for quantitative analysis.
